title: Bacterial infection in Ebola virus disease, Marburg virus disease, Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, and Lassa fever
abstract: Abstract Background Concern for bacterial coinfection in patients with high consequence viral infections (HCVIs) has made the empiric antibiotic administration the standard of care. However, the incidence, microbiology, and clinical significance of bacterial coinfection in HCVIs remain unclear. Methods We conducted a systematic review of case reports, cohort studies, and cross-sectional analyses describing bacterial coinfection in Ebola virus disease (EVD), Marburg virus disease (MVD), Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), and Lassa fever (LF). Data were extracted on study design, setting, diagnostic methods, pathogens, antibiotic use, and outcomes. Results Thirty publications met inclusion criteria. Bacteremia was most commonly reported among patients with CCHF (n = 46), followed by EVD (n = 16), MVD (n = 16), and LF (n = 2). Of 27 EVD patients treated outside Africa, seven (26%) had bacterial coinfection. Across HCVIs, bacteremia was detected a median of 11 days after symptom onset (range 0–23) and was associated with features of sepsis. Pathogens included enteric flora, healthcare-associated organisms, opportunistic pathogens, and zoonotic bacteria—most notably Brucella spp. Ceftriaxone was the most common empiric antibiotic but is predicted to have activity against a minority of bloodstream isolates. Mortality among coinfected patients with EVD or MVD was similar to those without bacterial coinfection, whereas coinfected CCHF patients had higher mortality than those without coinfection (15.5%; 95% CI 8.0–25.9% vs 5.7%; 95% CI 5.1–6.4%). Conclusions Despite being a major concern driving empiric antibiotic use, bacterial coinfection in HCVIs remains poorly described, precluding determination of its incidence or clinical significance. Prospective studies with standardized protocols for bacterial diagnosis and characterization of antimicrobial resistance are needed to guide antimicrobial strategies.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to clarify the incidence, microbiology, and clinical significance of bacterial coinfection in patients with high consequence viral infections (HCVIs), including Marburg virus disease (MVD), as concern for bacterial coinfection has driven empiric antibiotic administration despite unclear evidence.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A systematic review of case reports, cohort studies, and cross-sectional analyses was conducted to describe bacterial coinfection in MVD and other HCVIs, with data extracted on study design, setting, diagnostic methods, pathogens, antibiotic use, and outcomes.
analysis.methods: The review included studies describing bacterial coinfection in MVD, with data extraction focused on pathogens, diagnostic methods, antibiotic use, and outcomes, though specific protocols for bacterial diagnosis were not standardized across studies.
analysis.main_results: Among patients with MVD, 16 cases of bacteremia were reported; across all HCVIs, bacteremia was detected a median of 11 days after symptom onset and was associated with features of sepsis, with mortality among coinfected MVD patients similar to those without bacterial coinfection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that bacterial coinfection in HCVIs, including MVD, remains poorly described, precluding determination of its incidence or clinical significance, despite being a major concern driving empiric antibiotic use.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Findings highlight the need for prospective studies with standardized protocols for bacterial diagnosis and characterization of antimicrobial resistance to guide antimicrobial strategies in MVD and other HCVIs.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence strength is limited by the lack of standardized protocols for bacterial diagnosis and characterization of antimicrobial resistance across studies, with the reliance on case reports and cohort studies introducing potential bias and confounding.

Among MVD patients, 16 cases of bacteremia were reported, with bacteremia detected a median of 11 days after symptom onset and associated with sepsis features. Mortality in coinfected MVD patients was similar to non-coinfected cases. The study found that bacterial coinfection in HCVIs remains poorly characterized, despite driving empiric antibiotic use. Pathogens included enteric flora, healthcare-associated organisms, and opportunistic bacteria, with ceftriaxone being the most common empiric antibiotic but predicted to have limited activity against bloodstream isolates. The authors emphasize the need for prospective studies with standardized diagnostic protocols to guide antimicrobial strategies.

title: Marburg Virus: A Looming Threat Nigeria Cannot Ignore.
abstract: To the Editor: high population density, and concurrent Lassa fever and Mpox burdens make preparedness a national imperative [7]. The recent cross-sectional assessment by Oisakede et al. [8] offers empirical confirmation of this vulnerability. The study, conducted among 216 healthcare workers at Nigeria's national viral haemorrhagic fever reference centre (Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital), revealed that only 19 % of doctors and 10 % of nurses had received formal MVD training, and less than half felt adequately protected by personal protective equipment (PPE). Confidence in hospital readiness was significantly lower among doctors (32.5 %) than nurses (65.6 %), indicating institutional and role-specific disparities in outbreak preparedness.These empirical findings from Oisakede et al. [8] and the regional evidence base reveal a clear preparedness gap. While Nigeria benefits from a national Lassa fever infrastructure, this platform is yet to be fully extended to filoviruses like Marburg. The 2026 data provide a measurable baseline for monitoring progress and justify targeted capacity-building funding within the National Action Plan for Health Security (2026-2030). Preparedness is thus not merely theoretical; it demands investment in people, protocols and platforms. Leveraging the Oisakede et al. [8] evidence for policy advocacy strengthens the argument that Nigeria must institutionalise training, simulation, and infrastructure before the next filovirus crisis arrives. title: Digital Health for Pandemic Preparedness: A Critical Review of Innovations, Equity Gaps, and Governance in Infectious Disease Surveillance
abstract: Context: Recent infectious disease emergencies, including SARS-CoV-2, mpox (2022 - 2024), highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in US dairy cattle (2024 - 2025), and the Marburg virus in Rwanda (2024), have strained traditional surveillance systems. Digital health has been proposed as a paradigm shift; however, most reviews have focused on diagnostic accuracy while neglecting equity and governance. Evidence Acquisition: We conducted a structured thematic narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature published from January 2010 to March 2025, reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from February 5 to 18, 2025. Search keywords combined three concept blocks: (1) Digital-health technologies (artificial intelligence, machine learning, mHealth, eHealth, telemedicine, electronic health records, wearables, wastewater surveillance, genomic surveillance, natural-language processing); (2) infectious diseases (outbreak, pandemic, epidemic, COVID-19, Ebola, Zika, mpox, influenza, antimicrobial resistance, Marburg); and (3) public-health functions (surveillance, detection, forecasting, contact tracing, governance, equity). Full Boolean syntax is provided. Records were deduplicated in EndNote X20 and screened by 2 blinded reviewers in Rayyan (Cohen κ = 0.81). Empirical studies were appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, and reviews were appraised using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists. The synthesis followed Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis and was interpreted through sociotechnical systems and data justice lenses. Results: Of 1498 records, 142 studies met the inclusion criteria; 48% (69/142) were rated as high quality. The evidence base was heavily skewed regionally (high-income countries [HICs], 41%; sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia, 19%). No technology was universally superior. Artificial intelligence (AI) studies were concentrated in HICs (18/32, 56%), whereas short-message-service (SMS) mHealth studies were concentrated in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs; 15/25, 60%). Recurring barriers included algorithmic bias, fragmented interoperability, donor-dependent sustainability, and slow benefit-sharing of pathogen data with LMICs. Conclusions: Across 142 included studies the synthesis supports a measured conclusion: Digital health is necessary but not sufficient for pandemic preparedness. The patterns most consistently observed in the evidence — regional skew, recurring governance failures, donor-dependent sustainability, and design choices that determine equity outcomes — together indicate that equity, sustainability, and accountability are constituents of effectiveness rather than obstacles to it. The binding constraint is increasingly political and institutional will rather than analytic uncertainty.

title: Antibody Therapy Targeting GP in Treatment of Ebola Virus Infection
abstract: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is a severe and acute fatal disease caused by the Orthoebolavirus zairense (Ebola virus, EBOV), first identified in 1976. From 1976 to 2025, multiple Ebola virus disease outbreaks were documented, predominantly attributable to the Zaire ebolavirus (ZEBOV) species, followed by Orthoebolavirus sudanense (Sudan ebolavirus, SUDV), with a limited number of outbreaks associated with Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense (Bundibugyo ebolavirus, BDBV). As of 2025, numerous outbreaks caused by the EBOV have severely impacted public health and the global economy, particularly in West Africa. One of the response strategies has been the development of broad-spectrum neutralizing antibodies for prevention and treatment. ZMapp was the first antibody cocktail authorized for the emergency treatment of patients infected with ZEBOV. To date, two antibody-based therapeutics—Inmazeb and Ebanga—have been officially approved by the FDA in 2020 for the treatment of ZEBOV infection. Following the discovery of these ZEBOV-specific antibodies, numerous antibodies with broader antiviral spectra have been identified and are currently under development. This review summarizes neutralizing antibodies targeting seven key domains of the EBOV glycoprotein (GP), specifically: the glycan cap, GP1/head, base, fusion loop, GP1/core, GP1/2, and HR2/MPER (Heptad Repeat 2/Membrane-Proximal External Region). A deeper understanding of the characteristics of these neutralizing antibodies will accelerate the development of novel antibody therapies and provide guidance for the rational design of next-generation drugs against EBOV infection.

title: UNDERSTANDING LIPID-PROTEIN INTERACTIONS IN THE CONTEXT OF EBOLA AND MARBURG VIRUSES TO UNCOVER UNDERLYING MECHANISMS OF DISEASE PROGRESSION
abstract: Protein-lipid interactions are fundamental regulators of membrane-associated protein structure and function, thus influencing processes involving both viral life cycle and normal cellular functioning. Therefore, these interactions become important in understanding the underlying principles of progression of multitude of diseases. Viral matrix proteins are a fantastic model system to study these processes because these proteins rely heavily on host cellular membranes to coordinate trafficking and assembly. in this thesis, we have investigated the molecular mechanisms of membrane association of various proteins, with a focus on Ebola and Marburg virus matrix protein VP40.These viruses cause a highly fatal hemorrhagic fever and there is a dire need for finding ways to combat them, hence, learning how these viruses use their proteins to exploit host cellular membranes is a very important step in the battle against them. This knowledge has been further extended to the human parainfluenza virus 3 (HPIV-3) matrix protein M and the human protein ceramide kinase (CERK) to examine how they interact with certain lipids.With the help of mutagenesis, cellular assays and biochemical and biophysical approaches, this study has uncovered the essential roles of membrane binding residues of VP40 in coordinating multiple stages of viral life cycle. This has also identified critical residues in both proteins and indicated a difference in sensitivity towards mutations. We have also identified lipid binding modes of HPIV-3 M and CERK.Overall, this thesis highlights the importance of protein-lipid interactions as determinants of membrane-associated protein function and reveals how distinct molecular structure can achieve similar biological functions. These findings advance our understanding of viral assembly as well as a broader insight into lipid-dependent cellular processes.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand the molecular mechanisms of membrane association of viral proteins, particularly focusing on Ebola and Marburg virus matrix protein VP40, to uncover how these viruses exploit host cellular membranes in disease progression.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research investigated various proteins including Ebola and Marburg virus VP40, human parainfluenza virus 3 matrix protein M, and human protein ceramide kinase, using mutagenesis, cellular assays, and biochemical and biophysical approaches.
analysis.methods: The study employed mutagenesis, cellular assays, and biochemical and biophysical approaches to examine protein-lipid interactions and identify essential membrane binding residues in viral proteins.
analysis.main_results: The research identified essential roles of membrane binding residues in VP40 for coordinating multiple stages of the viral life cycle, critical residues in both proteins, differences in mutation sensitivity, and distinct lipid binding modes for HPIV-3 M and CERK.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight how distinct molecular structures can achieve similar biological functions through protein-lipid interactions, advancing understanding of viral assembly and lipid-dependent cellular processes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These insights provide a foundation for developing strategies to combat highly fatal hemorrhagic fevers caused by Ebola and Marburg viruses by targeting their exploitation of host cellular membranes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence strength is moderate as it focuses on molecular mechanisms without direct clinical applications or large-scale population data, though it provides detailed biochemical and biophysical analyses.

analysis.summary_en: This dissertation investigates protein-lipid interactions in Ebola and Marburg viruses to understand disease progression mechanisms. By studying viral matrix proteins like VP40 and comparing them with human proteins such as HPIV-3 M and CERK, the research identifies essential membrane binding residues critical for viral life cycle coordination. The findings reveal how distinct molecular structures achieve similar functions through lipid interactions, advancing knowledge of viral assembly and cellular processes. This work provides a scientific foundation for developing countermeasures against these highly fatal hemorrhagic fevers by targeting viral exploitation of host membranes.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解病毒蛋白膜关联的分子机制,特别关注埃博拉病毒和 马尔堡病毒 基质蛋白 VP40,以揭示这些病毒如何在疾病进展中利用 马尔堡病毒 细胞膜。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究利用诱变、细胞分析以及生化和生物物理方法研究了多种蛋白质,包括埃博拉病毒和 马尔堡病毒 VP40、人副流感病毒 3 基质蛋白 M 和人蛋白神经酰胺激酶。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究采用诱变、细胞测定以及生物化学和生物物理方法来检查蛋白质-脂质相互作用并鉴定病毒蛋白质中必需的膜结合残基。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究确定了 VP40 中膜结合残基在协调病毒生命周期多个阶段中的重要作用、两种蛋白质中的关键残基、突变 敏感性的差异以及 HPIV-3 M 和 CERK 的不同脂质结合模式。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现强调了不同的分子结构如何通过蛋白质-脂质相互作用实现相似的生物学功能,从而增进对病毒组装和脂质依赖性细胞过程的理解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些见解为制定策略通过针对 宿主 细胞膜的利用来对抗埃博拉和 马尔堡病毒 引起的高度致命的出血热提供了基础。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据强度中等,因为它侧重于分子机制,没有直接的临床应用或大规模人群数据,尽管它提供了详细的生化和生物物理分析。

source_body_en: Protein-lipid interactions are fundamental regulators of membrane-associated protein structure and function, thus influencing processes involving both viral life cycle and normal cellular functioning. Therefore, these interactions become important in understanding the underlying principles of progression of multitude of diseases. Viral matrix proteins are a fantastic model system to study these processes because these proteins rely heavily on host cellular membranes to coordinate trafficking and assembly. in this thesis, we have investigated the molecular mechanisms of membrane association of various proteins, with a focus on Ebola and Marburg virus matrix protein VP40.These viruses cause a highly fatal hemorrhagic fever and there is a dire need for finding ways to combat them, hence, learning how these viruses use their proteins to exploit host cellular membranes is a very important step in the battle against them. This knowledge has been further extended to the human parainfluenza virus 3 (HPIV-3) matrix protein M and the human protein ceramide kinase (CERK) to examine how they interact with certain lipids.With the help of mutagenesis, cellular assays and biochemical and biophysical approaches, this study has uncovered the essential roles of membrane binding residues of VP40 in coordinating multiple stages of viral life cycle. This has also identified critical residues in both proteins and indicated a difference in sensitivity towards mutations. We have also identified lipid binding modes of HPIV-3 M and CERK.Overall, this thesis highlights the importance of protein-lipid interactions as determinants of membrane-associated protein function and reveals how distinct molecular structure can achieve similar biological functions. These findings advance our understanding of viral assembly as well as a broader insight into lipid-dependent cellular processes.

title: Ebola Virus Disease in Africa: Recurrent Outbreaks, Continuing Public Health Threat, Medical Countermeasures, and One Health Perspectives
abstract: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is a zoonotic disease of great public health importance. It is characterized by a high case fatality rate, causes outbreaks, and can lead to major social and economic disruption. First recognised in 1976 in Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the disease has since emerged in different parts of Africa. The most significant outbreak occurred between 2014 and 2016 in West Africa. EVD is caused by species of the genus Orthoebolavirus, including Ebola virus, Sudan virus, and Bundibugyo virus. These viruses differ in fatality rates and in the availability of medical countermeasures. Fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir. Transmission to humans occurs through contact with infected animals, body fluids of infected persons, and contaminated environments, including during unsafe burial practices. The early stages present with non-specific symptoms, followed by gastrointestinal and hemorrhagic symptoms. Laboratory confirmation involves molecular, antigen-based, serological, and virological methods. Treatment options include supportive care, monoclonal antibodies for cases caused by Orthoebolavirus zaire, and vaccination. However, major gaps remain in the treatment and prevention of Sudan and Bundibugyo virus infections. Despite progress in EVD management, further research is needed to improve preparedness, diagnosis, treatment, and control. Therefore, this review discusses the etiology, epidemiology, transmission, pathogenesis, clinical spectrum, diagnosis, treatment, control, and One Health implications of Ebola virus disease, while highlighting existing knowledge gaps and future research needs.

title: Epidemiological Analysis of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak and Rapid Risk Assessment for North Africa and Europe
abstract: Abstract Background In 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) experienced the largest recorded outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, with epidemiologically linked importations and secondary transmission in Uganda. This study analysed the publicly reported trajectory and assessed the risk of introduction and onward transmission in North Africa and Europe. Methods Public surveillance reports from the World Health Organization (WHO), European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), Africa CDC, national ministries of health, and peer-reviewed sources were synthesised through 15–17 July 2026. Headline counts and crude case-fatality ratios were restricted to laboratory-confirmed cases. Average notification rates were calculated from cumulative DRC counts. Exact Poisson intervals used the Garwood method, and the June–July rate ratio was estimated on the log scale. Risk was assessed across introduction likelihood, conditional onward-transmission likelihood, impact, and confidence. Results By 15 July, the DRC had reported 2,124 confirmed cases and 828 deaths (crude confirmed-case fatality ratio, 39.0%) across 46 health zones in five provinces. Uganda had reported 20 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths: 15 imported infections and five secondary cases, with no documented community transmission. DRC notifications averaged 47.4 per day during 1–15 July versus 35.9 per day during 2–29 June (rate ratio 1.32; counting-model 95% interval 1.20–1.46). WHO reported that more than 80% of new cases were detected outside known contact lists, while 119 confirmed healthcare-worker infections and 36 deaths had occurred. Introduction likelihood was assessed as very low to low for North Africa and very low for the general European population; delayed recognition in routine healthcare was the principal scenario for limited secondary transmission. Interpretation Available indicators were inconsistent with effective control in eastern DRC at the data cut-off. Public reporting-date series cannot separate transmission from changing ascertainment, but they showed no sustained decline. Preparedness in North Africa and Europe should prioritise complete exposure histories, rapid isolation, validated diagnostics, protected clinical care, and contact management rather than reliance on border screening.

full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02432-1 News & views Viral infection Ebola virus persistence and the hidden cost of immune privilege Amal Fahmi, Isabel Schultz-Pernice & Marco P. Alves Human brain organoids reveal how Ebola virus establishes persistent infection within the immune-privileged environment of the central nervous system. The idea of immune privilege has reshaped our understanding of how the immune system is regulated across tissues. It is viewed as a state of selective immune tolerance characterized by tissue- and organ-specific immune regulation. Classic examples include the central nervous sys- tem (CNS), eyes and testes, where immune surveillance is present but constrained. These sites maintain a highly regulated immunological milieu through cellular barriers, local immunoregulatory mediators and context-dependent modulation of antigen presentation. While this restrained inflammatory tone is essential to preserve the function and integrity of indispensable tissues, it comes at a cost: the same features that limit immunopathology can also reduce pathogen clearance. As a result, immune-privileged niches may be co-opted by pathogens as long-term reservoirs and enable persistence despite systemic immune surveillance. Understanding how viruses exploit these specialized envi- ronments is therefore critical for defining the mechanisms underlying chronic infection and relapse. Numerous studies have characterized viral replication dynamics, transmission and evolution during acute Ebola virus (EBOV) infection. However, increasing evidence indicates that EBOV can persist during the chronic phase, with ongoing viral replication in survivors sup- porting the concept that persistence represents an active infection Check for updates Immune-privileged CNS • Restrained inflammation • Cellular barriers (for example, BBB and choroid plexus) • Antigen drainage (glymphatics and meningeal lymphatics) • Limited immune surveillance EBOV persistence in the brain Virus exploits immune privilege to establish long-term infection The hidden cost Chronic neuroinflammation Type I IFNs and inflammatory mediators Neuron Astrocyte Microglia Oligodendrocyte Defective viral genomes Viral evolution Persistent reservoirs Neuronal dysfunction and injury Fig. 1 | Immune privilege as a double-edged sword during EBOV persistence in the CNS. The CNS maintains a tightly regulated immune environment that limits inflammation and preserves tissue integrity. In human brain organoids, EBOV infects multiple neural cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia, via viral spread through budding and direct cell-to-cell transmission. Persistent infection is associated with viral evolution and accumulation of defective viral genomes, mechanisms thought to favour chronic low-level replication. In parallel, activated microglia produce pro- inflammatory mediators and type I interferons (IFNs) that may drive chronic neuroinflammation and neuronal injury. BBB, blood–brain barrier. nature microbiology News & views within immune-privileged reservoirs1. Among these niches, the CNS has emerged as a particularly clinically relevant site, as studies in non- human primates have demonstrated that replication-competent EBOV can remain in the brain after clearance from the periphery, leading to fatal relapses2. Yet the mechanisms underlying EBOV persistence in the human CNS remain poorly understood, leaving key questions unanswered regarding the neural cell populations that support long- term infection and the associated host responses. In this issue of Nature Microbiology, Widerspick and colleagues3 provide mechanistic insights on how orthoebolaviruses exploit the CNS’s immune-privileged status to establish long-term persistence. The authors developed a human brain organoid model that enables long-term analysis of orthoebolavirus infection in the human neural tissue and tested EBOV (species Orthoebolavirus zairense), Sudan virus (species Orthoebolavirus sudanense), Reston virus (species Orthoe- bolavirus restonense), and a related filovirus, Marburg virus (species Orthomarburgvirus marburgense). In these organoids, they show that EBOV can persist for up to 120 days within diverse neural cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, microglia and oligodendrocytes. This persistence, referring to the continued presence of infectious virus or viral genetic material beyond the acute phase of infection, suggests that EBOV can establish a sustained reservoir within human neural tissue. Mechanistically, the study shows that EBOV persistence relies on both canonical viral budding and direct cell-to-cell transmission through actin-dependent cellular projections and syncytia formation. Cell-to- cell spread is recognized as a potential mechanism of immune evasion, allowing viruses to disseminate while potentially reducing exposure to soluble immune mediators4. Within highly interconnected neural tissue, this mode of spread may be advantageous, as shown by our recent work demonstrating that monkeypox virus exploits neuronal connectivity to propagate while limiting immune exposure5. Widerspick and colleagues observed that long-term persistence of EBOV was associated with ongoing viral evolution together with the accumulation of defective viral genomes. Defective viral genomes are increasingly recognized as regulators of persistent infection because they can attenuate cytopathic replication while allowing for minimal levels of viral activity. By interfering with replication of full-length viral genomes, defective viral genomes have been proposed to modulate viral replication and host responses, potentially reducing cytopathic effects and contributing to persistence6. Importantly, the study iden- tifies marked cell type-specific differences in the host response to persistent EBOV infection. Whereas infected astrocytes remained comparatively quiescent, microglia mounted robust pro-inflammatory and type I interferon responses, identifying these cells as likely drivers of the chronic neuroinflammation associated with EBOV persistence. This observation reinforces the concept that immune privilege may support long-term viral maintenance while allowing inflammatory responses to emerge once local immune activation is engaged (Fig. 1). Similar patterns have been observed in other neurotropic viral infections. Replication-competent Zika virus, for example, can persist in the brains of surviving mice for more than 1 year within inflamma- tory foci enriched in activated microglia and astrocytes, where viral persistence is associated with chronic inflammation and neuronal injury7. More broadly, persistent viral reservoirs represent one of sev- eral proposed mechanisms contributing to post-acute sequelae of infection, including long COVID, in which sustained immune activation may result from a combination of viral persistence, immune dysregula- tion and other host factors8,9. Whether the mechanisms of CNS persis- tence identified for EBOV are conserved among other Orthoebolavirus species such as Bundibugyo virus — the driving pathogen of the current Ebola disease outbreak — remains unclear. Bundibugyo virus has shown evidence of CNS involvement in animal models, with viral antigen and RNA detected in CNS-associated tissues10,11, and long-term neurological sequelae reported in human survivors12. However, whether Bundibugyo virus establishes CNS persistence through similar cellular tropism and host–virus interactions remains unknown. Comparative studies will be required to determine whether CNS persistence represents a conserved feature across all orthoebolaviruses and to define the viral and host determinants that enable long-term infection within neural tissue. Although brain organoids provide a valuable platform to investi- gate EBOV persistence in human neural tissue, they remain a simplified representation of the CNS and do not fully recapitulate the complex immune, barrier and cellular interactions that shape viral persistence within the intact CNS. Consequently, caution is warranted when extrapo- lating these findings to human disease. This is particularly relevant given that the CNS maintains selective communication with the peripheral immune system through structures such as the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels, which facilitate antigen clearance and immune cross-talk between the brain and peripheral lymphoid organs. The meninges, choroid plexus and perivascular spaces are also recognized as neuroimmune hubs that coordinate immune surveillance, antigen presentation and leukocyte trafficking13. Addressing these ques- tions will be essential to determine whether EBOV persistence reflects escape from immune surveillance or an active adaptation to the CNS environment. Future organoid models incorporating cellular barriers, vascular components and peripheral immune cells will help determine how these virus–host interactions are shaped by neuroimmune com- munication and how EBOV establishes and maintains CNS reservoirs. They may also clarify whether microglia promote or restrict persistence and whether viral evolution within the CNS contributes to relapse or transmission. Collectively, these next-generation human brain models will provide a framework to investigate the mechanisms governing viral persistence in the CNS in a more physiologically relevant context. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how Ebola virus establishes persistent infection within the immune-privileged environment of the central nervous system, addressing the knowledge gap of viral exploitation of immune-privileged niches as long-term reservoirs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research utilized human brain organoids to investigate Ebola virus infection dynamics in the central nervous system, examining multiple neural cell types including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia.
analysis.methods: The study characterized viral replication dynamics, transmission mechanisms, and evolution during persistent infection, analyzing defective viral genomes and pro-inflammatory mediator production by activated microglia.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how Ebola virus establishes persistent infection in the immune-privileged central nervous system using human brain organoids. The research reveals that Ebola virus infects multiple neural cell types through budding and direct cell-to-cell transmission, with persistent infection associated with viral evolution and defective genome accumulation. The findings demonstrate that immune privilege enables viral persistence as an active infection, leading to chronic neuroinflammation and neuronal injury. This work provides critical insights into viral reservoirs in immune-privileged sites and informs therapeutic approaches for Ebola survivors.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解埃博拉病毒如何在中枢神经系统的免疫特权环境中建立持续感染,解决病毒利用免疫特权生态位作为长期 储存宿主 的知识差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究利用人脑类器官来研究中枢神经系统中的埃博拉病毒感染动态,检查多种神经细胞类型,包括神经元、星形胶质细胞、少突胶质细胞和小胶质细胞。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究描述了持续感染期间的病毒复制动力学、传播 机制和 进化,分析了缺陷病毒 基因组 和激活的小胶质细胞产生的促炎介质。
elements_zh.main_results: 在人脑类器官中,埃博拉病毒通过出芽和直接细胞间传播感染多种神经细胞类型,并与病毒进化相关的持续感染和缺陷病毒基因组的积累相关。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,免疫特权使埃博拉病毒能够作为一种主动感染持续存在,这代表了对病毒如何利用特殊环境来建立慢性感染和复发的新认识。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为监测在免疫特权部位持续存在病毒储存宿主的策略提供了信息,并强调了针对埃博拉幸存者慢性神经炎症和神经元损伤的治疗的需要。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 由于依赖类器官模型,证据强度中等,该模型可能无法完全复制体内人类中枢神经系统的复杂性。
